2.text: they invited the people, — husbands with young wives, fathers with grown-up daughters. All night

3.text: they sang and danced and played, till the time came to go home. Then they would choose such

4.text: women or girls as suited their fancy, and would detain them, of their own free will or by force.

5.text: A husband who came with a wife would return alone, or a father without his daughter, or a brother

6.text: without his sister. The women and girls had to stay with them as long as they remained in the

7.text: village. After a while they would leave the village, and everything in their houses would be left

8.text: to the women. Some of the husbands would receive them back, and some would not. In the

9.text: latter case the women had to live alone and be wretched. Oh, these husbands! How foolish they

10.text: were! It was not their will nor the woman’s will. The superiors gave the order, and what could

11.text: be done? Thus they lived in our country through the spring and the summer. When fall came,

12.text: they went to the sea with their dogs. They took with them the best men of all the country, —

13.text: those that knew the sea and were clever in travelling. When driving on the sea, they saw an island.

14.text: There were churches with golden tops, houses and people all of purest gold. When they came

15.text: nearer, an old woman came to meet them. The baron was a pipe-smoker, so she gave him a golden

16.text: pipe. Anjou took snuff. She gave him a snuff-box. Then she said, ‘I know you are seeking the

17.text: passage to America. Better go back. This is the limit of human travel. If you want to pass

18.text: on, you shall never go back.’ They held a council, and then turned from the island and went

19.text: across the sea. After a while they found open water. In the middle stood a tree, high up to the

20.text: very sky. This tree would bend down and enter the water. After a while it would emerge from

21.text: the water full of fish. And while it was swinging up high, all the fish were being consumed. They

22.text: felt afraid of this tree, and turned off to the right, toward the land. After a while they found

23.text: another island. It was quite deserted. Tobacco was growing there; and the leaves were so large,

24.text: that each one would suffice to swaddle a man’s head in it. They took some and left the island,

25.text: going to the land. At the place where they stopped the first night, a thundering noise came

26.text: suddenly from the direction of the island. The drivers were frightened, and woke them up. They

27.text: sat down upon the sledges, and the dogs ran away at a furious rate. Still the noise grew nearer and

28.text: nearer. Finally the ice began to heave and roll like billows. They drove on without sleeping or

29.text: eating, and at last reached the land. There they stopped to rest. When they awoke in the morning,

30.text: they saw that all the ice was broken, and gathered into icebergs. They came to the fortress (of

31.text: Nishne-Kolymsk), went to the church, and took a solemn oath to keep silence corcerning the things

32.text: they had seen on the sea, because they knew that if they should disclose these secrets, all the people

33.text: in the country must perish. So they kept their oath, and not until many years later did some old

34.text: men relate a part of their adventures.”

35.text: GENERAL CHARACTER OF CREOLE POPULATION. — The manners and the

36.text: ways of the Russian creole population, who represent on the Kolyma the

37.text: race of the conquerors, fully correspond to the kind of government they have.

38.text: I have mentioned before the extreme looseness as regards sexual life which

39.text: reigns in all Russian settlements of the arctic part of eastern Siberia, from

40.text: the mouth of the Yana to the southern part of Kamchatka. The people on

41.text: the Kolyma say, “Our water is of such quality that we cannot do otherwise.”

42.text: Perhaps in reality this easy excitability is influenced, not by the water, indeed,

43.text: but by the diet of fat fish which prevails on the Kolyma. Mr. Jochelson

44.text: believes that the sexual looseness of the Russians has arisen under Yukaghir

45.text: influence, and even asserts that the Russian term “maiden-children” is a term

46.text: adopted from the Yukaghir maˊrxid-uˊo (i.e., “child born by a maiden”).¹ It

47.text: cannot be denied that the Yukaghir influence on the Russian population was
